transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doctor. I'm here because... well, lately my mind just feels like it's full of fog. It's thick, you know? Like those mornings when I walk to the library. I've been working at the same branch for, gosh, must be fifteen years now. We used to have this old oak tree out front that would look so beautiful in the mist, but they chopped it down last year because the roots were getting into the plumbing. A real shame, if you ask me. But anyway, yeah, the fog in my head. I can't even keep my place in my old cataloguing notes anymore. I'll be looking right at them, and it's just... blank. And then I can't even decide what simple thing to do next. Just yesterday, I stood in the breakroom for ten minutes trying to figure out if I should make tea or just go back to my desk. My coworker, Brenda—she makes this awful smelling herbal tea, by the way—she had to ask me if I was okay.
Over the past few weeks, have you been feeling noticeably sad, down, or have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose I have. Most days lately, I just sit at my kitchen table in the mornings... it's this old formica table I bought at a garage sale back in '98. Or maybe it was '99? It has those metal legs that scrape on the linoleum if you don't put those little felt pads on them. I keep meaning to buy more of those pads at the hardware store, but I never seem to get around to it. 

But anyway, I just sit there, and it feels like... I don't know, like all the color has just gone out of everything. Even my old watercolor books. I used to love painting little landscapes on my days off, but now, looking at them just makes me feel so heavy inside instead of interested. I don't even want to open them. My sister got me a new set of brushes for my birthday last year, real nice sable ones. They cost a pretty penny, let me tell you. She lives out in Portland now, where it rains all the time, so she paints a lot of gray skies, which I always thought was a bit gloomy. But I haven't even taken those brushes out of the plastic... I just sit there at that table feeling heavy.

Can you tell me exactly when you first started noticing this mental fog and trouble concentrating—was it something that came on fairly suddenly in the past few weeks, or has it been gradually getting worse over many months or years?

Well, let me think... I'd say it's been about three months now. Most days, anyway. It started right around the time I began getting all my paperwork together to finally leave the library. Which, let me tell you, is quite the process. The human resources department there is really just one woman, Susan. She's a lovely lady, makes a wonderful pecan pie for the holiday potluck every year, but her filing system is absolutely from the dark ages. 

I kept telling her, Susan, you really need to digitize these retirement forms. My nephew over in Seattle does that kind of computer work for big companies. He actually just bought a boat with all the money he makes doing it. A sailboat, if you can believe it. I told him I'd never go out on it because I get terribly seasick, even on those little ferry rides across the bay. The smell of the water and the rocking just turns my stomach right upside down, always has since I was a little boy... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Right, the fog and feeling so down. Yes, it hasn't been years or anything like that. Just about three months, right when I started preparing to leave the library.

Besides losing your train of thought, have you noticed yourself actually forgetting things that happened recently—like a conversation you had, an appointment, or getting confused about the day or where you were—things that are separate from just having trouble concentrating?

No, I don't think so... I haven't forgotten any appointments or anything like that. Well, except for my dental cleaning last week, but that doesn't really count because they called to reschedule it anyway. My dentist, Dr. Miller, he's been trying to get me to use this new electric toothbrush. He says it's better for the gums, but honestly, I just can't stand the vibration. It rattles right up into my jaw. It reminds me of when they used to do construction on the street outside my old apartment building. They were tearing up the pavement for three weeks straight, starting at six in the morning! Can you imagine? I had to start sleeping with a pillow over my head. I tried those little foam earplugs, the orange ones, but they always fall out in the middle of the night and then you're just searching around in the dark for them... 

But no, my memory itself is fine. I know what day it is, and I don't forget conversations. It's really just the... the fog, and not being able to focus on what's right in front of me.
Since you started preparing for retirement, have you been feeling anxious, worried, or on edge about this change, separate from the low mood and fog you described?

Well, no, not really anxious. I mean, I'm not sitting around worrying about it or feeling on edge. It's just... it's just that heavy feeling. But you know, speaking of being on edge, my neighbor's dog has been barking at all hours lately. It's a little terrier mix, I think. Cute as a button, but loud! It reminds me of a dog my aunt used to have when I was a kid. Buster, his name was. Buster used to chase the mailman every single day. The mailman, Mr. Henderson, he was a saint, really. He'd always bring a pocket full of those little milk bone treats just to keep Buster from nipping at his ankles. Mr. Henderson retired years ago, moved down to Florida, I think. Or maybe it was Arizona? Somewhere warm, anyway. I've never been to Arizona, but I hear the sunsets are just spectacular over the desert... 

But anyway, no, I haven't been feeling worried or anxious about leaving the library. Just sad and foggy, like I said.
Over these past three months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up much earlier than usual?

Well, my sleep hasn't been great, actually. I go to bed feeling completely exhausted, but then my eyes pop open at around four in the morning. Every single night. And I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, thinking about what on earth I'm supposed to do with myself now. It's so quiet at that hour. You know, the only thing you can hear is the refrigerator humming. I bought that refrigerator about ten years ago from Sears before they closed down the one at the mall. It was a floor model, so I got a really good deal on it. It's one of those ones with the freezer on the bottom, which is supposed to be better for your back so you don't have to bend over as much to get the milk. My chiropractor, Dr. Evans, he always says bending at the waist is the worst thing you can do. He told me I should be doing these core exercises, but honestly, who has the energy for that? He has this poster in his office of a spine, and it always makes me think of those Halloween decorations... 

But, oh, right, the sleep. Yes, waking up at four and just lying there thinking about my days now. It's been happening a lot.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient endorses a 3-month history of persistently depressed mood ('heavy feeling'), anhedonia (loss of interest in painting, a previously enjoyed activity), difficulty concentrating and indecisiveness ('mental fog'), and early morning awakening (waking at 4am nightly). These core depressive symptoms co-occur without evidence of true memory impairment, disorientation, or anxiety symptoms, arguing against a cognitive or anxiety disorder. Although the onset coincides with the psychosocial stressor of retirement preparation, the symptom cluster meets full criteria for a major depressive episode rather than a milder stress-reactive adjustment disorder, and there is no medical explanation offered for the mood/cognitive symptoms. Severity specifiers (mild/moderate/severe) and psychotic features were not clearly established, so the episode is coded as unspecified.
